title: Unregistered amendment
scenario: Chairperson: “At our Standard Module scheme’s general meeting on 18 March, 42 of 60 voters supported a special resolution replacing the visitor-parking by-law. The committee began enforcing the replacement on 1 April, but the new community management statement was not lodged until 29 July. Three infringement letters were issued during those 120 days.”
instructions: “What should the body corporate manager advise the chairperson about the replacement by-law’s operation during that period?”

title: Late CMS lodgement
scenario: Secretary: “Owners passed a special resolution changing the balcony appearance by-law on 7 February by 38 votes to 6. The solicitor completed the new community management statement on 20 May, but it was lodged on 16 June, more than 3 months after the meeting. Titles Queensland recorded it 8 days later.”
instructions: “What should the body corporate manager advise the secretary in this situation?”

title: Committee-made house rule
scenario: Committee Member: “Our 84-lot Accommodation Module scheme has a gym used from 5 a.m. until 10 p.m. The committee voted 5 to 2 on 12 August to introduce a ‘house rule’ prohibiting anyone under 16 from entering. It was emailed to all occupiers 3 days later, but the recorded by-laws contain no age restriction.”
instructions: “What should the body corporate manager advise the committee member about the house rule?”

title: Tenant-only restriction
scenario: Resident Manager: “By-law 14 allows owners to book the rooftop area for 6 hours but limits tenants to 2 hours. The scheme contains 96 lots, of which 61 are rented. Last Saturday, a tenant’s 4-hour booking was rejected even though 3 booking periods remained available and no owner had requested them.”
instructions: “What should the body corporate manager advise the resident manager about applying this by-law?”

title: Residential letting restriction
scenario: Chairperson: “Our 110-lot residential scheme adopted a by-law on 4 April requiring every tenancy to run for at least 90 days. The motion passed by 67 votes to 18, and the new CMS was recorded on 30 May. An owner has now accepted three separate 14-night bookings beginning on 12 December.”
instructions: “What should the body corporate manager advise the chairperson about enforcing the by-law?”

title: Moving bond
scenario: Treasurer: “By-law 9 requires a refundable $1,500 bond, a $220 lift-booking fee and 7 days’ notice for every move. During the past 6 months, 11 occupiers paid both amounts. A new tenant has supplied 10 days’ notice but refuses to pay either charge before moving in on 23 October.”
instructions: “What should the body corporate manager advise the treasurer about applying the by-law?”

title: Automatic penalty
scenario: Secretary: “Our Commercial Module scheme’s loading-zone by-law states that a person who parks longer than 30 minutes must pay the body corporate $250 for each occurrence. One delivery vehicle remained for 74 minutes on 3 September and 58 minutes on 5 September. The committee has issued a $500 invoice.”
instructions: “What should the body corporate manager advise the secretary about the invoice?”

title: Blanket animal prohibition
scenario: Chairperson: “Our CMS contains a by-law saying no animal of any kind may be kept in a lot. A lot owner applied on 2 June to keep one desexed cat weighing 4.8 kilograms. The cat would remain indoors, and the owner supplied 3 references, but the committee rejected the request 6 votes to 1.”
instructions: “What should the body corporate manager advise the chairperson about the committee’s decision?”

title: Animal approval conditions
scenario: Lot Owner: “The committee approved my 9-kilogram dog on 14 January subject to 8 conditions. Condition 6 requires me to carry the dog across all common property, including a 95-metre driveway and 3 flights of stairs. I am 72 years old, and the committee gave me 7 days to confirm compliance.”
instructions: “What should the body corporate manager advise the lot owner about the approval condition?”

title: Assistance animal
scenario: Occupier: “I moved into lot 28 on 1 September with an accredited assistance dog that is 6 years old and weighs 27 kilograms. The recorded by-law limits animals to 10 kilograms and requires prior committee approval. Yesterday, I received a notice giving me 14 days to remove the dog.”
instructions: “What should the body corporate manager advise the occupier in this situation?”

title: Visitor parking by owner
scenario: Chairperson: “Our parking by-law reserves 12 marked bays for visitors and prohibits residents from using them. An owner parked in bay 7 for 45 minutes on Monday, 70 minutes on Wednesday and 32 minutes on Friday while loading medical equipment. The committee wants to issue one continuing contravention notice.”
instructions: “What should the body corporate manager advise the chairperson about the proposed notice?”

title: Isolated noise event
scenario: Committee Member: “A tenant held a party from 8 p.m. until 12.20 a.m. on 17 July. Security recorded 3 complaints and attended twice, but there have been no earlier or later complaints during the tenant’s 14-month occupancy. The committee proposes giving a continuing contravention notice requiring the noise to cease.”
instructions: “What should the body corporate manager advise the committee member about the proposed notice?”

title: Repeated intermittent breach
scenario: Secretary: “An occupier has held noisy gatherings on 4 Saturdays during the past 7 weeks. Each gathering ended before security arrived, with the most recent finishing at 11.35 p.m. The by-law prohibits unreasonable noise, and the committee voted 4 to 1 to issue a notice requiring immediate cessation.”
instructions: “What should the body corporate manager advise the secretary about the appropriate response?”

title: Notice sent to the owner
scenario: Property Manager: “A tenant in lot 46 has allegedly breached the pool by-law on 5 occasions over 21 days. The committee addressed the contravention notice only to the interstate owner and emailed me a copy 2 days later. The named tenant, who signed a 12-month lease, received nothing directly.”
instructions: “What should the body corporate manager advise the property manager about the notice?”

title: Copy to lot owner
scenario: Secretary: “The committee personally served a future contravention notice on a tenant on 6 August after 3 pool incidents. The tenant’s landlord lives overseas. A copy was sent to the landlord 19 days later, after the tenant allegedly repeated the conduct twice during that interval.”
instructions: “What should the body corporate manager advise the secretary about the enforcement process?”

title: Defective contravention notice
scenario: Chairperson: “Our committee sent a letter dated 9 May stating, ‘You are breaching the parking by-laws and have 48 hours to comply.’ The CMS contains 4 separate parking provisions. The letter did not identify one provision, describe the vehicle or explain the alleged conduct. Proceedings were authorised 6 votes to 0.”
instructions: “What should the body corporate manager advise the chairperson about relying on the letter?”

title: Owner’s enforcement request
scenario: Lot Owner: “I lodged the approved by-law notice with the committee at 9 a.m. on 2 March after documenting 7 parking incidents over 18 days. On 17 March, the secretary told me the matter would be discussed at a meeting in another 3 weeks. No contravention notice has been issued.”
instructions: “What should the body corporate manager advise the lot owner in this situation?”

title: Informal complaint only
scenario: Occupier: “I emailed the committee 5 times between 1 and 24 April about a neighbour’s barking dog. I attached 3 audio recordings and a 16-day diary, but I did not use an approved form. The committee declined to act, and I lodged a conciliation application 8 days later.”
instructions: “What should the body corporate manager advise the occupier about the application?”

title: Urgent safety breach
scenario: Chairperson: “An occupier has chained an electric bicycle across the only fire-exit gate on level 4. It has obstructed the 1.2-metre exit for 3 nights, and 26 residents use that level. The occupier refuses to move it, but the committee has not yet issued a contravention notice.”
instructions: “What should the body corporate manager advise the chairperson about responding to the situation?”

title: Indoor smoking prohibition
scenario: Secretary: “On 11 May, owners passed a special resolution prohibiting smoking everywhere within the scheme, including inside all 73 lots. The vote was 51 in favour and 9 against. The CMS was recorded on 22 June, and the committee has since received 4 complaints about smoking inside lot 19.”
instructions: “What should the body corporate manager advise the secretary about enforcing the prohibition?”

title: Balcony smoking by-law
scenario: Lot Owner: “A by-law recorded on 3 August prohibits smoking on every balcony between 6 a.m. and midnight. My balcony is 14 square metres and forms part of my lot. I smoked there twice at 5.40 a.m., and the committee has received 3 complaints from the lot directly above.”
instructions: “What should the body corporate manager advise the lot owner about the recorded by-law?”

title: Appearance approval
scenario: Committee Member: “By-law 8 requires written approval before changing a lot’s external appearance. An owner installed 6 black-framed windows on 10 September, replacing white frames, without approval. The committee later rejected retrospective approval 3 votes to 2, although 17 other lots have dark frames approved under earlier applications.”
instructions: “What should the body corporate manager advise the committee member about enforcing the by-law?”

title: Solar installation
scenario: Chairperson: “An owner applied to install 12 solar panels, each measuring 1.7 metres by 1.1 metres, entirely within the roof boundary of their lot. By-law 16 prohibits visible solar equipment. The committee rejected the application 5 votes to 1 because the panels would be visible from 8 balconies.”
instructions: “What should the body corporate manager advise the chairperson about the by-law?”

title: Exclusive-use grant
scenario: Secretary: “At an extraordinary general meeting on 15 February, owners voted 36 to 2 to give lot 9 exclusive use of 22 square metres of garden. The scheme has 40 voters, and the owner of lot 14 opposed the motion. The committee nevertheless signed a licence for 10 years beginning 1 March.”
instructions: “What should the body corporate manager advise the secretary about the arrangement?”

title: Exclusive-use reallocation
scenario: Lot Owner: “The recorded CMS allocates car space 18 exclusively to my lot. At a meeting on 6 June, 44 of 48 voters supported reallocating it to lot 31, while I voted against the motion. The new allocation is intended to operate for 5 years and the committee has issued me 14 days’ notice to vacate.”
instructions: “What should the body corporate manager advise the lot owner about the reallocation?”

title: Exclusive-use maintenance charge
scenario: Treasurer: “An exclusive-use by-law gives lot 12 sole use of a 38-square-metre courtyard and states that its owner must maintain the tiles and drainage. Repairs costing $7,800 became necessary after 6 years. The owner says the body corporate must pay because the courtyard remains common property.”
instructions: “What should the body corporate manager advise the treasurer about responsibility for the repair cost?”

title: Small Schemes Module enforcement
scenario: Lot Owner: “Our Small Schemes Module scheme has 5 lots and no committee. The body corporate passed a resolution by 3 votes to 1 on 8 April to issue a notice about repeated obstruction of the driveway. The secretary says only a committee can authorise enforcement and has taken no action for 21 days.”
instructions: “What should the body corporate manager advise the lot owner about the enforcement decision?”

title: Specified Two-lot scheme
scenario: Lot Owner: “Our Specified Two-lot scheme has lots with interest entitlements of 55 and 45. The other owner has parked 2 trailers on common property for 47 consecutive days, contrary to the recorded by-law. I sent 3 written requests, the latest 16 days ago, but no joint decision is possible.”
instructions: “What should the body corporate manager advise the lot owner about pursuing the alleged breach?”

title: Pre-1997 scheme by-laws
scenario: Chairperson: “Our scheme was registered on 9 October 1989. Its one-page CMS, recorded on 12 July 2000, lists no by-laws. The committee assumes the standard by-laws in the current Act apply and has issued 4 parking notices during the past 6 months under the standard parking provision.”
instructions: “What should the body corporate manager advise the chairperson about identifying the applicable by-laws?”

title: Registered but potentially invalid rule
scenario: Secretary: “A by-law recorded on 25 November requires committee consent before any owner may sell or lease a lot. It also requires a $900 processing fee and gives the committee 30 days to decide. Two owners complied last year, but a third signed a 24-month lease without seeking consent.”
instructions: “What should the body corporate manager advise the secretary about enforcing the recorded by-law?”

title: Assignment consent
scenario: Chairperson: “Our 118-lot Accommodation Module scheme received an assignment request on 4 September. Settlement is proposed for 18 October, and the agreement has 17 years remaining. The buyer has managed a 42-room motel for 3 years but has never operated a community titles scheme. Four of our seven committee members want consent made conditional on the buyer accepting twelve new weekly reporting duties not found in the agreement.”
instructions: “What should the body corporate manager advise the chairperson about the proposed response to the assignment request?”

title: Top-up motion
scenario: Caretaker: “My agreement in this 86-lot Standard Module scheme expires on 30 June 2034. I submitted an AGM motion 48 days before the financial year ended, requesting a 5-year extension and offering to pay up to $6,500 of the body corporate’s legal costs. The AGM notice provides for an ordinary resolution by open ballot, permits proxies and does not identify a returning officer.”
instructions: “What should the body corporate manager advise the caretaker about the proposed AGM process?”

title: Alleged non-performance
scenario: Committee Member: “The caretaker receives $142,000 a year under an agreement running until 2041. Over the last 11 weeks, owners have lodged 23 complaints about leaves in the pool area. The duty schedule requires inspection “as reasonably necessary” but gives no cleaning frequency. Five of seven committee members voted to stop the next two monthly payments unless the area is serviced every weekday.”
instructions: “What should the body corporate manager advise the committee member in this situation?”

title: Option exercise after expiry
scenario: Caretaker: “My Commercial Module agreement began on 1 July 2011 for 15 years. It contained one 5-year option exercisable by written notice between 9 and 6 months before expiry. I emailed the chairperson on 15 February 2026, but the contractual window closed on 31 December 2025. Since 1 July, the body corporate has paid three monthly invoices of $9,240 each.”
instructions: “What should the body corporate manager advise the caretaker about the status of the arrangement?”

title: Reallocating levies
scenario: Treasurer: “Our Standard Module scheme has 40 lots and contribution schedule entitlements totalling 1,000. The proposed administrative fund budget is $320,000. Twenty-four lots each have an entitlement of 15, while sixteen each have an entitlement of 40. At the AGM, 21 voters supported charging every lot $8,000 because the committee considers equal charging fairer and easier to explain.”
instructions: “What should the body corporate manager advise the treasurer about the levy resolution?”

title: Special contribution outside the budget
scenario: Chairperson: “A retaining wall failed 6 months after our AGM. The accepted repair quote is $186,000, but the sinking fund contains only $74,000 and the approved budget has no allocation for the work. Our committee spending limit is $35,000. Six of seven committee members voted to issue a special contribution in three instalments without calling a general meeting.”
instructions: “What should the body corporate manager advise the chairperson about funding the repair?”

title: Adjusting an AGM budget
scenario: Treasurer: “The AGM agenda proposes a sinking fund budget of $285,000. During the meeting, owners approved an agenda motion replacing a $90,000 lift project with a $123,000 proposal. There were 38 voters present, and 22 then supported increasing the budget to $318,000. Another owner argues that any change to the circulated budget automatically requires a later extraordinary general meeting.”
instructions: “What should the body corporate manager advise the treasurer about the budget adopted at the AGM?”

title: Early-payment discount
scenario: Lot Owner: “My quarterly contribution of $3,600 was due on 1 August and carried a 20 per cent discount. I paid $2,880 on 31 July, but $420 in recovery costs from a levy dispute 2 years ago remained on my account. The body corporate applied my payment to those older costs first and now says I lost the $720 discount.”
instructions: “What should the body corporate manager advise the lot owner about the disputed discount?”

title: Balcony membrane responsibility
scenario: Lot Owner: “My apartment is in a 64-lot building format plan. Water entered the lot below after 82 millimetres of rain on 14 January. The engineer attributes 70 per cent of the problem to a failed original balcony membrane and 30 per cent to tiles I installed 4 years ago. The repair quote is $28,600, and the committee says the entire balcony is my responsibility.”
instructions: “What should the body corporate manager advise the lot owner about responsibility for the repair?”

title: Roof within a lot boundary
scenario: Chairperson: “Our 22-lot townhouse scheme is registered under a standard format plan. Lot 7’s roof began leaking on 3 March, and a plumber’s report dated 9 March attributes the damage to 18 cracked original tiles above that lot. The owner obtained a $16,400 quote and says the body corporate must pay because the roof is visible from common property.”
instructions: “What should the body corporate manager advise the chairperson about the roof repair?”

title: Utility infrastructure serving two lots
scenario: Owner: “A wastewater pipe runs beneath my courtyard before branching to Lots 12 and 13. The blockage occurred 6 metres before the branch, and the plumber charged $4,950 for excavation and repairs. My exclusive-use by-law, registered 8 years ago, says I must maintain the courtyard surface but says nothing about underground pipes. The committee has invoiced the full amount to my lot.”
instructions: “What should the body corporate manager advise the owner about the repair charge?”

title: Urgent works exceeding authority
scenario: Caretaker: “At 2:15 am on Saturday, a common-property pump failed and water rose 18 centimetres in the basement. I accepted a contractor’s $31,800 emergency quote without contacting the committee. My agreement authorises urgent expenditure up to $7,500, and the committee spending limit is $25,000. The contractor completed the work within 9 hours and prevented water reaching the electrical switchboard.”
instructions: “What should the body corporate manager advise the caretaker about the unauthorised expenditure?”

title: Allocation of insurance excess
scenario: Treasurer: “A washing-machine hose installed inside Lot 18 failed after 14 months, damaging that lot and three common hallways. The accepted insurance claim is $47,000 with a $7,500 water-damage excess. The insurer attributes the event to sudden hose failure and identifies no maintenance defect. By a four-to-three vote, the committee charged the entire excess to Lot 18.”
instructions: “What should the body corporate manager advise the treasurer about allocating the insurance excess?”

title: Building valuation and underinsurance
scenario: Chairperson: “Our 96-lot building format plan was valued for insurance at $38 million on 12 June 2021. The current policy remains at $41 million, but a replacement-cost assessment obtained on 25 September 2026 recommends $57 million. Renewal is 19 days away, and the insurer has quoted an additional annual premium of $46,000. The committee wants to defer the increase until the next AGM in 5 months.”
instructions: “What should the body corporate manager advise the chairperson about the proposed deferral?”

title: Premium allocation between lots
scenario: Commercial Lot Owner: “Our building format plan has 30 residential lots and 4 shops. Contribution schedule entitlements total 1,200, while interest schedule entitlements total 2,000. The shops hold 620 interest entitlements but only 180 contribution entitlements. The annual building premium is $214,000, and the AGM resolved to allocate it using contribution entitlements because that produces lower charges for the shops.”
instructions: “What should the body corporate manager advise the commercial lot owner about the premium allocation?”

title: Improvement affecting insurance risk
scenario: Committee Member: “An owner installed two 13.5-kilowatt-hour batteries and a 22-kilowatt electric-vehicle charger in a basement exclusive-use space. Approval was given 7 months ago, subject to three electrical certificates, but only one certificate is on file. The insurer’s renewal questionnaire asks about battery systems installed during the previous 12 months, and four committee members want the question left unanswered.”
instructions: “What should the body corporate manager advise the committee member about the renewal questionnaire?”

title: Committee member conflict
scenario: Secretary: “Our seven-member committee is choosing between three landscaping quotations: $64,000, $71,500 and $79,200. The chairperson owns 40 per cent of the company that submitted the $64,000 quote but disclosed this only after discussion began. Five members, including the chairperson, voted for that contractor. The committee spending limit is $85,000.”
instructions: “What should the body corporate manager advise the secretary about the committee decision?”

title: Committee composition
scenario: Returning Officer: “At the AGM of our 112-lot Standard Module scheme, owners elected nine committee members: three executive members and six ordinary members. Candidates ranked eighth and ninth each received 31 votes. The chairperson says the larger committee should stand because 74 voters approved a procedural motion permitting nine positions before nominations closed.”
instructions: “What should the body corporate manager advise the returning officer about the election outcome?”

title: Restricted committee issue
scenario: Chairperson: “At last year’s AGM, owners resolved that any decision concerning the rooftop telecommunications lease must be made by general meeting. The lease now has 3 years remaining and produces $48,000 annually. The tenant offered a further 7-year term with rent increasing by 4 per cent each year. Six of seven committee members voted to accept the offer before it expired at 5 pm.”
instructions: “What should the body corporate manager advise the chairperson about the committee’s acceptance?”

title: Two-lot decision deadlock
scenario: Owner of Lot One: “Our scheme has only 2 lots and operates under the Specified Two-lot Schemes Module. Lot One has 60 contribution entitlements and Lot Two has 40. A common driveway requires $26,000 of repairs, and the contractor’s quote remains open for 21 days. I support the work, but the other owner refuses to approve any expenditure above $10,000 despite two engineering reports recommending prompt repair.”
instructions: “What should the body corporate manager advise the owner of Lot One about resolving the decision?”

title: Staged expenditure
scenario: Committee member: “We’re a 24-lot scheme under the Standard Module, and our committee spending limit is $5,000. We want to refurbish the entrance foyer. The tiling is quoted at $3,400, lighting at $2,100 and painting at $1,600, all including GST. We could approve each contractor under a separate committee motion over the next three months.”
instructions: “What should the body corporate manager advise the committee member about the committee’s authority in this situation?”

title: General meeting has already refused the proposal
scenario: Committee member: “At our general meeting 6 weeks ago, owners considered a $4,800 garden upgrade and the ordinary resolution was defeated by 18 votes to 11. We have 36 lots and a committee spending limit of $8,000. The same landscaper has now reduced the proposal to $4,500, and four committee members want to approve it.”
instructions: “What should the body corporate manager advise the committee member about the committee’s authority in this situation?”

title: Expenditure within the dollar limit but outside the budget
scenario: Committee member: “Our 40-lot Standard Module scheme has a committee spending limit of $9,000. Three committee members want to approve an unplanned drainage investigation costing $6,600 including GST. The current administrative fund budget contains $2,000 for drainage expenses, and only $900 of that allocation remains unspent.”
instructions: “What should the body corporate manager advise the committee member about the committee’s authority in this situation?”

title: Committee improvement to common property
scenario: Committee member: “Our Standard Module scheme has 30 lots and a committee spending limit of $12,000. We’re proposing new decorative lighting on common property at a total installed price of $8,700 including GST. It isn’t replacing existing lighting. Five of our seven voting committee members support proceeding, and no similar improvement has been approved this financial year.”
instructions: “What should the body corporate manager advise the committee member about the committee’s authority in this situation?”

title: Spending limit and GST
scenario: Committee member: “Our 28-lot Accommodation Module scheme has a committee spending limit fixed at $7,500. The committee received a lift-repair quotation for $7,200 plus 10 per cent GST. There is sufficient money in the approved maintenance budget, and five of the seven voting committee members support accepting the quotation.”
instructions: “What should the body corporate manager advise the committee member about the committee’s authority in this situation?”

title: No committee spending limit set
scenario: Committee member: “We have a 19-lot Standard Module scheme. The body corporate has never passed an ordinary resolution setting a different committee spending limit. Yesterday, four of the seven voting committee members supported accepting a common-property plumbing quotation for $3,950 including GST. The approved budget has $6,500 available for this work.”
instructions: “What should the body corporate manager advise the committee member about the committee’s authority in this situation?”

title: Major spending and quotations
scenario: Committee member: “Our 14-lot Standard Module scheme has a committee spending limit of $18,000, while no alternative major spending limit has ever been set. We have one quotation for $12,400 including GST to replace failed common-property equipment. Six of seven voting committee members want to accept that quotation immediately.”
instructions: “What should the body corporate manager advise the committee member about the committee’s authority in this situation?”

title: Owner seeks exclusive use through the committee
scenario: Committee member: “An owner has asked us to give Lot 17 exclusive use of two common-property car spaces for 5 years. The owner will pay $3,000 upfront and spend another $4,500 installing security equipment. Five of our seven voting committee members support the proposal, and the scheme contains 42 lots.”
instructions: “What should the body corporate manager advise the committee member about the committee’s authority in this situation?”

title: Altering rights created by a general meeting
scenario: Committee member: “Eight months ago, the body corporate passed a general meeting motion approving operating rules for 26 storage cages on common property. The committee now wants to change one eligibility condition for the remaining 9 cages. Four of seven voting committee members support the change, and 17 cages have already been allocated under the approved arrangements.”
instructions: “What should the body corporate manager advise the committee member about the committee’s authority in this situation?”

title: Contract commitment exceeding the spending limit
scenario: Committee member: “Our 55-lot Standard Module scheme has a committee spending limit of $15,000. A contractor has offered cleaning services at $4,200 every quarter under a 12-month agreement, with four equal payments. The first payment fits comfortably within the current budget, and six of seven voting committee members want to sign the agreement this week.”
instructions: “What should the body corporate manager advise the committee member about the committee’s authority in this situation?”

title: Committee attempts to make a new by-law
scenario: Committee member: “Our 70-lot scheme has received 12 written complaints about bicycles being stored in corridors over the past 5 months. The registered by-laws do not specifically prohibit bicycles there. Six of seven voting committee members have voted to create a new rule imposing a $150 charge whenever a bicycle is found in a corridor.”
instructions: “What should the body corporate manager advise the committee member about the committee’s authority in this situation?”

title: Emergency expenditure above the usual limit
scenario: Committee member: “Our 32-lot Standard Module scheme has a committee spending limit of $7,000. At 2 am, a common-property water main ruptured and water began entering 3 lots. Emergency isolation and repairs were quoted at $11,800 including GST. Four committee members authorised the contractor to start immediately to prevent further building damage.”
instructions: “What should the body corporate manager advise the committee member about the committee’s authority in this situation?”

title: Layered scheme calculation
scenario: Committee member: “Our principal body corporate has 6 lots. Five are subsidiary community titles schemes containing 18 lots each, while the remaining lot is not a community titles scheme. No ordinary resolution has ever changed the committee spending limit. The committee proposes common-property repairs costing $17,900 including GST, and sufficient budgeted funds are available.”
instructions: “What should the body corporate manager advise the committee member about the committee’s authority in this situation?”

title: Commercial Module assumption
scenario: Committee member: “Our scheme is registered under the Commercial Module and contains 16 lots. The committee wants to authorise $21,000 of common-property mechanical repairs from an approved $28,000 maintenance allocation. Someone has objected that the committee can spend only $3,200 because that equals $200 for each lot.”
instructions: “What should the body corporate manager advise the committee member about the committee’s authority in this situation?”

title: Authority delegated to the committee
scenario: Committee member: “At a general meeting 4 months ago, owners approved a $24,000 maximum budget for replacing 8 common-property doors and authorised the committee to select from 3 specified contractors. The committee now prefers a fourth contractor quoting $21,500. Five of seven voting committee members support that contractor, whose proposal remains below the approved maximum.”
instructions: “What should the body corporate manager advise the committee member about the committee’s authority in this situation?”
